title: A Book sent to bring people from darkness into light.
subtitle: What the Quran is for
then: The surah opens with letters whose meaning is known to Allah, a cue to stop and listen. Then it says why the Book came: {idea}to bring mankind out of darkness into light{/idea}, by their Lord's permission. Ibn Kathir notes it was sent to all people, Arabs and non-Arabs alike.
now: Some nights everything feels dark at once: the debt, the argument, the doubt. You do not need ten fixes. {reward}You need one light to walk toward.{/reward} The Book in your phone's app is that light.
old: My problems are too many and too tangled for one Book to touch.
new: Darkness comes in many forms; the Quran is the one way out into light.
try: Open the Quran today and read just one page slowly, asking Allah to bring you into the light.

title: Everything in the heavens and earth belongs to Him.
subtitle: The owner of the path
then: Verse 1 named the path of the Mighty, the Praised. This verse says who He is: {idea}Allah, to whom everything in the heavens and earth belongs{/idea}. Ibn Kathir links it to the Prophet ﷺ being sent to all people by the Owner of all. {trap}Woe to those who refuse.{/trap}
now: You call it my car, my house, my time, my body. Every one of those was given and can be taken. {idea}Nothing in your hands is really yours.{/idea} That is not a threat; it is a reason to hold things lightly.
old: What I have is mine to use however I want.
new: Everything belongs to Allah; I am trusted with some of it for a while.
try: Pick one thing you call yours and use it today in a way that pleases its Owner.

title: Loving this world more, and bending the path for others.
subtitle: Three marks of being far astray

row.title: far astray
sub: a long way from the light

then: The surah introduction says this was revealed late in Makkah, when {trap}opposition to the Prophet ﷺ was at its worst{/trap}. The verse names those who choose this life over the next, {trap}hold others back from Allah's path{/trap}, and try to make it look crooked.
now: A friend starts praying again and you make a joke about it. You call the deen too strict to someone curious. You put the weekend plans ahead of everything. {idea}Small habits, but they point the wrong way.{/idea}
old: Putting this world first only affects me.
new: Loving this world most can make me a block on others' path to Allah.
try: Encourage one person today in something good they are trying, without any joke.

title: Every messenger spoke his people's language.
subtitle: Clarity is part of Allah's kindness
then: Ibn Kathir says Allah is kind to His creation, sending messengers {idea}from among the people, speaking their language{/idea}, so they could understand. Each was sent to his own people, and he cites a hadith that {reward}the Prophet ﷺ was sent to all mankind{/reward}.
now: You tell yourself the Quran is hard to understand, so you leave it. Yet there are translations on your phone, in your own language, right now. {idea}The message was made clear for you.{/idea} The next step is yours.
old: Religion is too complicated for someone like me.
new: Allah made His message clear in a language I can understand.
try: Read the translation of one short surah today in your own language.

title: Remind them of the days of Allah.
subtitle: Lessons for the patient and the grateful
then: Like the Prophet ﷺ, Musa was sent to bring his people from darkness into light. Ibn Kathir says the days of Allah are {reward}His favours: rescue from Pharaoh, the path through the sea, shade, manna and quails{/reward}. He cites a hadith: {idea}the believer is patient in hardship and grateful in ease, and both are good for him.{/idea}
now: You remember every bad day in detail and forget the time the surgery went well, the job offer that came at the last minute. {reward}Your own days of Allah.{/reward} Recalling them makes you steady now.
old: I mostly remember what went wrong.
new: Remembering what Allah has done for me makes me patient and grateful.
try: Write down three times Allah rescued you or gave you something unexpected.

title: Remember the favour of being rescued.
subtitle: Musa reminds his people of Pharaoh's cruelty and Allah's rescue
then: Musa told his people: remember Allah's favour {idea}when He saved you from Pharaoh's people{/idea}, who were {trap}killing your sons and sparing your daughters{/trap}. Ibn Kathir says the 'great trial' may mean the cruelty, or the rescue as a favour too great to thank fully. Both meanings can be held.
now: You survived a very hard year: the illness, the abusive job, the debt. Now life is calmer and you rarely think back. {reward}The rescue is a favour worth remembering.{/reward} It is also a test of what you do now.
old: That hard time is behind me; best not to think about it.
new: Both the hardship and the rescue were from Allah, and both ask for gratitude.
try: Thank Allah out loud today for one specific hard time He brought you through.

title: If you are grateful, He will give you more.
subtitle: Allah's open promise about thanks
then: Musa reminded his people of Allah's declaration. Ibn Kathir says it means: {reward}if you appreciate My favour, I will give you more of it{/reward}. If you deny it, {trap}the punishment may be losing that favour{/trap}. He cites a hadith that a person can be denied provision because of a sin.
now: You open the fridge, sigh, and close it. You scroll through a friend's holiday photos and feel your own life is small. Meanwhile you have a roof, a phone, people who love you. {reward}Thanks opens the door to more.{/reward}
old: I will be grateful once I have enough.
new: Gratitude comes first, and more follows it.
try: Before sleeping tonight, thank Allah for five specific things from today.

title: Allah does not need your thanks; you do.
subtitle: Free of need, and still worthy of all praise

row.title: Allah needs it
sub: I am doing Him a favour

then: Musa told his people that even if they and everyone on earth disbelieved, {idea}Allah is free of need and worthy of praise{/idea}. Ibn Kathir cites the hadith in Muslim: if all creation had the most pious heart, {idea}it would add nothing to His dominion{/idea}.
now: Sometimes you pray like you are doing Allah a favour, ticking a box for Him. On a lazy day you feel He owes you for showing up. {reward}Every prayer and every thanks is a gift to yourself.{/reward}
old: My worship is something I give Allah.
new: Allah needs nothing from me; my worship and thanks are for my own good.
try: In your next prayer, remind yourself before you start: this is for me, not for Him.

title: Hands over their mouths: refusing to even listen.
subtitle: Nations whose number only Allah knows

row.title: hands to mouths
sub: we deny it, we doubt it

then: Ibn Kathir says only Allah knows how many such nations there were. Their messengers came with clear proofs. {trap}They put their hands to their mouths{/trap}: scholars said this means silencing the messengers, rejecting them, or biting their hands in anger. {trap}We are in deep doubt, they said.{/trap}
now: Someone you trust gently points out a habit that is hurting you. Before they finish, you are already shaking your head. {idea}Refusing to hear is a choice, not a doubt.{/idea}
old: I have doubts, so I do not have to listen.
new: Real doubt listens; covering my ears is just refusal.
try: Next time someone gives you advice today, let them finish before you answer.

title: Can there be doubt about the Creator of the heavens?
subtitle: He calls you in order to forgive you
then: The messengers asked: {idea}can there be doubt about Allah, Creator of the heavens and earth?{/idea} Ibn Kathir says most nations accepted a Creator but called on others too. The invitation was gentle: {reward}He calls you to forgive you{/reward}. They replied: you are just men like us; {trap}bring us a miracle of our choosing{/trap}.
now: You picture Allah's call as a list of rules aimed at catching you out. Read it again: {reward}He calls you so that He may forgive you.{/reward} The adhan five times a day is an invitation, not an accusation.
old: Religion is mainly about rules and blame.
new: Allah's call is an invitation to forgiveness.
try: Make istighfar once today, picturing it as accepting His invitation.

title: We are only human, but Allah chooses whom He favours.
subtitle: The messengers did not claim more than they were
then: Ibn Kathir notes the messengers agreed: {idea}we are human like you{/idea}. But Allah gives prophethood to whom He chooses. They could not produce signs on demand, {idea}only by Allah's permission{/idea}. Then they turned to their own: {reward}let the believers rely on Allah{/reward}.
now: Someone says you are no better than them, so who are you to talk about faith. {idea}You can agree and stay humble.{/idea} You never claimed to be special. You just rely on Allah and keep going.
old: To speak about faith, I have to prove I am better than others.
new: I can admit I am ordinary and still rely fully on Allah.
try: If you are challenged about your faith today, answer humbly and say inside: on Allah I rely.

title: Why would we not rely on the One who guided us?
subtitle: Trust and patience under pressure

row.title: patience and trust
sub: on Allah let the trusting rely

then: The messengers continued: {reward}how could we not trust Allah, when He has guided us?{/reward} Ibn Kathir says they promised to {idea}bear with patience{/idea} the foolish actions and abusive words thrown at them.
now: Your relatives mock your hijab or your beard at every family dinner. You can feel the reply ready on your tongue. {idea}The One who guided you is enough to lean on.{/idea} Patience here is strength, not weakness.
old: If people keep hurting me, I need to fight back.
new: The One who guided me is worth trusting, and patience is my answer.
try: Next time someone needles you about your faith, smile, stay silent, and say Hasbunallah inside.

title: Return to our ways or leave: Allah answered the threat.
subtitle: When the pressure is to conform or be pushed out
then: The surah introduction says this verse reflects late Makkah, when {trap}the persecution of the Muslims was at its worst{/trap}. Ibn Kathir lists the same threat against Shu'ayb and Lut. {idea}Allah answered the messengers: We will destroy the wrongdoers.{/idea}
now: Your friend group says: drink with us or stop coming. Your workplace hints you should drop the prayer breaks. {idea}Conform or be left out is an old pressure.{/idea} The messengers held on, and Allah had the last word.
old: If I do not go along with them, I will lose my place.
new: Pressure to give up my faith is old, and Allah stands with those who hold on.
try: Choose one small way to stay true today where you usually give in to pressure.

title: The land goes to those who fear standing before Allah.
subtitle: The promise after the threat of expulsion
then: The threat was expulsion. The answer: {reward}We will settle you in the land after them.{/reward} Ibn Kathir says this came true when the Prophet ﷺ, once driven from Makkah, later had it opened to him. {idea}It is for whoever fears standing before Allah.{/idea}
now: You are the one pushed out of the team for refusing to fudge the numbers. It feels like losing. {reward}Allah's promise is longer than this week.{/reward} Fear of standing before Him is what keeps your place secure.
old: The ones pushing me out will always have the upper hand.
new: Allah gives the land to those who fear standing before Him.
try: Before one hard choice today, picture standing before Allah, then choose.

title: They asked for victory, and the arrogant lost.
subtitle: When both sides call for the decision
then: After the threats and the promise, {idea}a decision was sought from Allah{/idea}. {trap}Every stubborn, arrogant tyrant who refused His Oneness was brought to loss.{/trap} Ibn Kathir places this within the same story of messengers and their nations.
now: You are in a long argument with your brother, and you are sure you are right, so you will not budge an inch. Ask yourself honestly: {trap}is this conviction, or just stubbornness?{/trap} Pride loses even when it wins.
old: Holding my ground no matter what shows strength.
new: Stubborn pride is what fails in the end; humility before truth wins.
try: In one disagreement today, say: you may be right, let me think about it.

title: Ahead of the arrogant lies Hell.
subtitle: What waits after the loss
then: The verse continues about the arrogant tyrant who refused the messengers. {trap}Hell lies ahead of him, and a foul drink.{/trap} The Quran mentions it soberly, as a warning, so those who hear it can turn back before then.
now: You think of consequences only as far as next month. The verse lifts your eyes further. {idea}What I do now is carried forward.{/idea} That is a warning and also a mercy: there is still time to change course.
old: Whatever happens to me happens in this life only.
new: My choices reach beyond this life, so I take them seriously now.
try: Ask Allah tonight to protect you from the Fire, and name one habit you will drop to that end.

title: Death from every side, yet no dying.
subtitle: A suffering with no exit

row.title: I will deal with it later

then: The description continues for the arrogant who rejected the messengers. {trap}Death comes at him from every side, yet he does not die{/trap}, and still more lies ahead. It is told plainly so that people listening in Makkah, and today, {idea}take the warning while life remains{/idea}.
now: There are nights you wish a problem would just end. This verse describes a place where nothing ends. {reward}Today, every door of repentance is still open.{/reward} Walk through one.
old: There will always be a way out later.
new: The way out is now, in this life, through turning to Allah.
try: Make sincere tawbah today for one specific sin, and ask Allah for His mercy.

title: Deeds without foundation are ashes in a storm.
subtitle: When work is built on nothing
then: Ibn Kathir says this parable is for those who rejected their Lord and built their deeds {trap}on a groundless base{/trap}. They thought they had something, but on the Day {trap}it scattered like ashes in the wind{/trap}, just when they needed it most. He links it to charity spoiled by showing off.
now: You give to charity and post about it. You help a neighbour and mention it later at dinner. {idea}Ask what is under the deed.{/idea} Sincerity for Allah is the ground that keeps it from blowing away.
old: A good deed is good, whatever the reason behind it.
new: Deeds need faith and sincerity underneath, or they blow away.
try: Do one good deed today that no one will ever know about.

title: The One who made the heavens can replace you.
subtitle: Creation in truth, and our dependence
then: Ibn Kathir says this proves the resurrection: the One who made the vast heavens and earth {idea}can easily bring the dead back{/idea}. And if people defy Him, {trap}He can remove them and bring another creation{/trap}. He links it to: you are the ones in need of Allah.
now: You start to feel your mosque, your family, your workplace would fall apart without you. {idea}Allah's work does not depend on any one of us.{/idea} That is humbling, and also freeing: serve because it is an honour, not because He needs you.
old: Things would fall apart without me.
new: Allah needs no one; being used for His work is an honour.
try: Do one act of service today and thank Allah for letting you be the one to do it.

title: None of it is hard for Allah.
subtitle: Replacing a people, raising the dead: easy for Him
then: The short verse closes the thought before it. Ibn Kathir says removing people and bringing others {idea}is not hard or impossible for Allah. It is easy for Him.{/idea} It was said to people in Makkah who doubted they could ever be raised again.
now: You look at your marriage, your debts, your son's anger, and think: this is beyond fixing. For you, maybe. {idea}Not for Him.{/idea} The One who raises the dead can mend what feels dead in your life.
old: Some of my problems are simply impossible.
new: Nothing is difficult for Allah, so I never stop asking.
try: Ask Allah today for the one thing you had stopped asking for because it seemed impossible.

title: Followers and leaders stand together, and no one can help.
subtitle: Blind following, examined on the Day
then: Ibn Kathir describes everyone appearing before Allah {idea}on a flat plain with no cover{/idea}. The followers say to the leaders they obeyed: {trap}can you protect us now?{/trap} The leaders reply: if Allah had guided us, we would have guided you. {trap}There is no escape for us.{/trap}
now: You do something because your favourite influencer does it, or the uncle everyone listens to says it is fine. {idea}No one you follow can stand in for you.{/idea} Pick who you follow as if you will meet them there.
old: If I am following someone respected, it is on them.
new: I answer for my own choices, including whom I follow.
try: Unfollow or mute one voice today that pulls you away from Allah.

title: Shaytan's last speech: do not blame me, blame yourselves.
subtitle: He only invited; you said yes
then: After judgement is done, Shaytan addresses his followers. {reward}Allah's promise was true{/reward}; his was a lie. Ibn Kathir explains: {trap}I had no proof and no power over you. I only called and you answered.{/trap} He disowns them and cannot help.
now: Midnight, alone with your phone, the thought arrives. It does not push your thumb. {idea}It only invites.{/idea} The one who will later say do not blame me is counting on you saying yes now.
old: Shaytan made me do it.
new: Shaytan only invites; the choice to answer is mine.
try: Next time a bad whisper comes, say A'udhu billah and do something else for five minutes.

title: Their greeting in the Garden is: Peace.
subtitle: The other side of the same Day
then: Right after Shaytan's bitter speech, the scene turns. Ibn Kathir notes it is the moment judgement is complete. {reward}Those who believed and did good enter gardens with rivers beneath, forever, by their Lord's permission.{/reward} {idea}Their greeting there is peace.{/idea}
now: Your home has days of shouting and slammed doors. Your work has days of blame. {reward}Imagine a place where every word is peace.{/reward} You can practise its greeting now, sincerely, at your own front door.
old: Peace is just a word people say out of habit.
new: Salam is the language of Paradise, and I can speak it here.
try: Say Assalamu alaykum warmly to everyone in your home today, meaning it.

title: A good word is a tree with deep roots and high branches.
subtitle: La ilaha illallah, planted in the heart
then: Ibn Abbas said the good word is {idea}La ilaha illallah{/idea}, and the good tree is the believer. Ibn Kathir cites Bukhari: the Prophet ﷺ asked about a tree like a Muslim, whose leaves do not fall. Young Ibn Umar thought of the answer but was too shy to say it. {reward}It is the date palm.{/reward}
now: You say La ilaha illallah in prayer every day without noticing. Try picturing it as a seed going deeper each time, while your kindness at work and patience at home grow upward like branches. {idea}Root and branch, one tree.{/idea}
old: Saying the shahadah is just a formula.
new: The shahadah is a root that grows into everything I do.
try: Say La ilaha illallah slowly ten times today, thinking about its meaning.

title: It gives fruit in every season.
subtitle: A believer's good never stops
then: The good tree of the last verse {reward}gives fruit at all times, by its Lord's permission{/reward}. Ibn Kathir says this describes the believer, {idea}whose good works rise to heaven by day and by night, summer and winter{/idea}. Allah gives parables so people remember.
now: You are generous in Ramadan and stingy by Shawwal. Kind when rested, short when tired. {reward}A date palm does not take a season off.{/reward} Small steady fruit, even on hard days, is the goal.
old: I do good when I am in the mood or the season is right.
new: A believer gives some fruit in every season, even small.
try: Choose one tiny daily good, like a morning dhikr, and do it today even if you are tired.

title: A bad word is a tree with no roots.
subtitle: Disbelief has nothing to stand on
then: Ibn Kathir says this tree describes {trap}disbelief, which has no base and no stability{/trap}. Anas said it is the colocynth, a bitter plant. {trap}Cut from its root, lying on the ground{/trap}, its works do not rise.
now: Some ideas in your feed sound exciting: a trend, a new life philosophy, a cynical joke about faith. Push on them and there is nothing under them. {idea}Ask of every idea: where is its root?{/idea}
old: A popular idea must have something solid behind it.
new: Ideas cut off from Allah have no root, however tall they look.
try: Next time an idea grabs you online, ask one question: what is this built on?

title: Allah holds believers steady with the firm word.
subtitle: Steady here, and steady in the grave
then: After the parable of the two trees, this verse says Allah keeps believers firm with that good word. Ibn Kathir cites Bukhari: {reward}when the Muslim is questioned in the grave, he testifies La ilaha illallah and that Muhammad ﷺ is Allah's Messenger.{/reward} {idea}That is the firm word.{/idea}
now: The doctor's face changes as she reads the results. Your hands go cold. What comes out of your mouth in that moment is what you have practised. {reward}Allah steadies the tongue that has said His name often.{/reward}
old: I will find the right words when the hard moment comes.
new: The word I repeat now is the one Allah makes firm for me later.
try: Ask Allah today: O Allah, keep me firm with the firm word in this life and the next.

title: They traded Allah's blessing for ingratitude.
subtitle: Swapping a gift for its opposite
then: Ibn Abbas said this refers to the people of Makkah. Ali said {reward}the blessing was faith, which came to the leaders of Quraysh{/reward}, and they {trap}exchanged it for disbelief and led their people to ruin{/trap}. Ibn Kathir adds the Prophet ﷺ was sent as a blessing to all mankind.
now: You were raised hearing the Quran at home, and now it sits unopened. The masjid is a five-minute walk and you have not been in months. {reward}Faith within reach is a blessing.{/reward} Leaders of a home lead others too.
old: Being born near faith is just background.
new: Faith within reach is a blessing I can either keep or trade away.
try: Use one blessing of faith near you today: the nearby masjid, the Quran on your shelf.

title: A wretched place to settle.
subtitle: Where the trade ends
then: The verse names the home of ruin that the leaders led their people into. {trap}It is Hell, a wretched place to settle.{/trap} It is stated briefly and soberly, a warning to people in Makkah who still had time to choose.
now: You plan where you will live, which school, which neighbourhood, for years ahead. {idea}The last home is the one that matters most.{/idea} The choices that lead there are made in ordinary days like this one.
old: I will think about the final home much later.
new: Where I end up is shaped by the small choices I make today.
try: Make the dua today: O Allah, I ask You for Paradise and seek refuge with You from the Fire.

title: Enjoy for now, but the destination is set.
subtitle: Rivals to Allah, and a brief enjoyment
then: Ibn Kathir says they {trap}set up partners to Allah and called people to worship them{/trap}. The Prophet ﷺ is told to say: enjoy yourselves. It is a warning, not permission. He links it to: {idea}We let them enjoy a little, then they return to Us.{/idea}
now: The weekend plan, the new car, the trip. None of it is wrong. But if it all quietly becomes the point of life, {idea}enjoyment turns into a rival{/idea}. Enjoy, and remember where you are heading.
old: Enjoying life now is all that really counts.
new: Enjoyment is brief; what I put in Allah's place decides my end.
try: Notice one pleasure today that you lean on too much, and thank Allah for it out loud.

title: Pray and give now, before a Day with no deals.
subtitle: A message to My servants who believe
then: After the warning, a gentle turn: {idea}tell My servants who believe{/idea}. Ibn Kathir says pray on time with humility, and spend on relatives and others. Qatadah said friendships made for Allah last; {trap}others will be cut off{/trap}. On that Day no ransom or bargain is accepted.
now: You know the right people, you can negotiate any deal, you have a cousin in every office. {idea}None of that works on that Day.{/idea} What works is the two rakahs you prayed and the money you quietly gave.
old: My network and my bargaining will always get me through.
new: Prayer and giving now are what count on the Day of no deals.
try: Give a small charity today in secret, and pray your next prayer on time.

title: Rain, fruit, ships and rivers, all put to your service.
subtitle: Look at what you use every day
then: Right after telling believers to pray and give, the verse reminds them who provides. Ibn Kathir lists {reward}rain bringing fruits of many colours and tastes, seas that carry ships between lands, rivers for drinking and farming{/reward}. {idea}It is Allah who made all of it serve people.{/idea}
now: The banana on your breakfast table crossed an ocean in a container ship. The tap water came from a river you have never seen. {reward}Every bite and sip passed through His favour.{/reward}
old: Supermarkets and pipes just work; there is nothing to notice.
new: Everything that feeds me runs by Allah's command.
try: At your next meal, think of one step that brought the food to you, and say Alhamdulillah.

title: Sun, moon, night and day run on schedule for you.
subtitle: The clock you never wound
then: The list of favours continues into the sky. Ibn Kathir says {reward}the sun and moon keep their courses{/reward}, and night and day each lengthen and shorten in turn. He links it to: the sun does not overtake the moon, {idea}each floats in its orbit{/idea}.
now: Your alarm goes off at six because you trust the sun will rise. You plan Ramadan by a moon you never moved. {reward}Your whole calendar rests on His favour.{/reward}
old: Sunrise and sunset are just how things are.
new: The sun, moon, night and day were set running for me by Allah.
try: Watch the sunset or sunrise today for one minute and remember who set it running.

title: Try to count His blessings and you will fail.
subtitle: Given more than asked, and still ungrateful
then: After the list, the conclusion: {reward}if you count Allah's favours, you could never finish{/reward}. Ibn Kathir cites the Prophet's ﷺ dua: All praise is Yours, never enough. He reports Dawud asked: {idea}how can I thank You, when my thanks is also Your favour?{/idea}
now: You spend twenty minutes listing what is wrong in your life to a friend. Try listing what is right and you stop at breath, eyesight, one person who loves you, and realise {reward}the list has no end{/reward}.
old: I have a good idea of what Allah has given me.
new: His favours outnumber my counting, so gratitude never finishes.
try: Set a timer for two minutes and list blessings out loud without stopping.

title: Ibrahim asked for a safe city and a protected family.
subtitle: The founder of Makkah prays
then: Ibn Kathir says this was said to the idol worshippers of Makkah: {idea}the House was built on worship of Allah alone{/idea}, and its founder Ibrahim prayed against idols. Allah accepted his dua for safety. Ibn Kathir notes {reward}a person praying should also ask for their parents and children{/reward}.
now: You pray quickly for your exam, your job, your health. Ibrahim prayed for the city and his sons, and for their faith most of all. {reward}Add your children and your home to your dua.{/reward}
old: My dua is mostly about my own needs.
new: Like Ibrahim, I pray for my family's faith and my home's safety too.
try: Tonight add one line to your dua: O Allah, keep me and my children far from worshipping other than You.

title: Whoever disobeys me, You are still Forgiving, Merciful.
subtitle: Ibrahim leaves the stubborn to Allah's mercy
then: Ibn Kathir says Ibrahim disowned idol worship but {reward}left those who disobeyed to Allah{/reward}, like Isa's words: if You forgive them, You are the Mighty, the Wise. He reports that {idea}the Prophet ﷺ recited both, raised his hands, and said: O Allah, my Ummah, my Ummah.{/idea}
now: A sibling has walked away from the deen, and part of you wants to write them off. Ibrahim's words show another way. {reward}Leave them to the Forgiving, the Merciful, and keep praying.{/reward}
old: Those who reject the truth deserve to be written off.
new: I can stand by the truth and still leave people to Allah's mercy.
try: Make dua tonight, by name, for someone who has turned away from faith.

title: A barren valley, chosen so they would pray.
subtitle: Ibrahim's family by the Sacred House
then: Ibn Kathir says Ibrahim made this dua after the House was built. He settled family in a valley with no crops {idea}so they could establish prayer{/idea}. He asked that {reward}hearts incline to them and fruits reach them{/reward}. Allah answered: fruit of every kind is brought to Makkah, though none grows there.
now: You are choosing where to live: the bigger flat far from any masjid, or the smaller one near. Ibrahim chose by one question. {idea}Where will my family be able to pray?{/idea} Provision followed.
old: I choose where to live by comfort and price.
new: Like Ibrahim, I can choose for prayer first and trust Allah for provision.
try: Ask yourself one honest question: what in my home helps my family pray? Improve one thing.

title: You know what we hide and what we show.
subtitle: Ibrahim's sincerity before his Lord

row.title: Allah
sub: nothing hidden in earth or sky

then: Ibn Jarir explains Ibrahim meant: {idea}You know the intention behind my dua for this town, that I seek Your pleasure sincerely.{/idea} He left his family in a barren valley. {reward}Allah knew exactly why.{/reward}
now: You made a hard decision: moved away, left a job, said no to a family plan. People misread it. {reward}Allah knows what you meant.{/reward} You do not have to win every explanation.
old: If people misunderstand my intentions, I have failed.
new: Allah knows what I hide and what I show; that is enough.
try: Before one action today, set your intention privately for Allah alone.

title: Children in old age: my Lord hears every dua.
subtitle: Ibrahim thanks Allah for Isma'il and Ishaq
then: Ibn Kathir says Ibrahim {reward}praised Allah for giving him children after he had grown old{/reward}. He notes Isma'il was thirteen years older than Ishaq. Ibrahim's lesson: {idea}He accepts the dua of those who call on Him.{/idea}
now: You have been asking for something for years: a child, a spouse, healing, a way out of debt. People hint it is too late. {idea}Ibrahim was answered in old age.{/idea} Keep asking, and praise Him for what has already come.
old: If it has not happened by now, it never will.
new: My Lord hears every dua, and His timing has no age limit.
try: Begin your next dua with praise for one answered prayer, then ask again.

title: Make me one who keeps up the prayer, and my children too.
subtitle: Ibrahim asks for prayer before anything else

key.label: What he wanted for his children

then: After thanking Allah for his sons, Ibrahim asks: {idea}make me one who establishes prayer, preserving its obligations, and my offspring too{/idea}. Ibn Kathir says he then asked Allah to {reward}accept all the duas he had made{/reward}.
now: You pray for your children to get into a good school, find a good job, marry well. Ibrahim, a prophet, still asked to be made one who prays. {reward}Ask for prayer for yourself and them first.{/reward}
old: My children will pick up prayer on their own.
new: Prayer for me and my children is worth asking Allah for every day.
try: Memorise this dua today: Rabbi ij'alni muqeem as-salati wa min dhurriyyati.

title: Forgive me, my parents, and all the believers.
subtitle: A dua that widens the circle
then: Ibrahim ends his prayer by asking forgiveness {idea}for himself, his parents and all the believers{/idea}, for the Day of reckoning. Ibn Kathir notes he said this {trap}before he disowned his father{/trap}, once it became clear his father was an enemy of Allah.
now: You make dua after prayer and it is a short list about your own week. Add your mother and father, living or gone. Then add every believer, including the stranger in the next row. {reward}A wide dua, said in seconds.{/reward}
old: My dua is about me and my needs.
new: My dua can hold my parents and every believer too.
try: After your next prayer, say: Rabbana ighfir li wa li walidayya wa lil mu'mineen.

title: Allah is never unaware of what wrongdoers do.
subtitle: Delay is not forgetting
then: Allah tells the Prophet ﷺ: {idea}do not think Allah is unaware of what the wrongdoers do.{/idea} Ibn Kathir says the delay is not neglect; {idea}Allah keeps full account of it{/idea}, until a Day when eyes stare in horror.
now: The landlord who cheated you is doing fine. The colleague who lied about you got promoted. It eats at you. {idea}Nothing was missed.{/idea} And the same verse is a mirror: what wrong of mine is quietly on record?
old: If wrongdoers get away with it, Allah must not care.
new: Allah sees every wrong; delay is not forgetting, for them or for me.
try: Let go of one grudge today by handing it to Allah, and fix one wrong of your own.

title: Rushing forward, eyes fixed, hearts empty.
subtitle: The terror of the Day of Gathering
then: Ibn Kathir says people will rise from their graves and {trap}hurry to the Gathering, heads raised, eyes staring, afraid to blink{/trap}. Their hearts are empty from fear. He adds: {idea}we seek refuge with Allah from this end.{/idea}
now: You know the feeling of a racing heart before a big interview, a blank mind in an exam. Multiply that. {reward}The calm you build now with prayer and repentance is preparation.{/reward}
old: Thinking about that Day is just frightening.
new: Remembering that Day helps me prepare while I still have calm days.
try: Say today, sincerely: O Allah, I seek refuge with You from the terror of that Day.

title: Give us a little more time, they will plead.
subtitle: The request that comes too late
then: The Prophet ﷺ is told to warn people of the Day when they will say: {trap}our Lord, delay us a little; we will answer Your call.{/trap} Ibn Kathir links it to: my Lord, send me back. They are reminded that {idea}they once swore their life would never end{/idea}.
now: You say: next Ramadan I will be serious, after the wedding, after this project. {idea}The little more time you would beg for later is today.{/idea}
old: I will answer Allah's call once things settle down.
new: The extra time I would beg for later is the time I have now.
try: Pick one thing you keep postponing for Allah, and start it today in a small way.

title: You lived in their houses and saw what happened.
subtitle: Lessons all around, and examples given
then: Ibn Kathir explains: {idea}you saw or heard what happened to earlier nations who rejected their messengers{/idea}, yet {trap}you drew no lesson{/trap}. He links it to: perfect wisdom, but the warnings did not benefit them.
now: You watched a friend's health fall apart from a habit you share. You saw a family split over money. {idea}The lessons are around you, sometimes in your own house.{/idea} Seeing is not enough. Learning is.
old: What happened to others will not happen to me.
new: The examples around me are lessons meant for me.
try: Think of one cautionary story from someone close to you, and take one lesson from it today.

title: Their plots, however huge, are known to Allah.
subtitle: Even mountain-moving schemes are in His hand
then: Ibn Kathir places this within the same passage about those who wronged themselves. {trap}They planned their plot{/trap}, but {idea}their plot was with Allah{/idea}, fully known and in His control. Even a plan big enough to shift mountains could not escape Him.
now: Someone with more money and lawyers is coming after you over the inheritance. It feels like a mountain. {idea}Their plan is known to Allah, and in His hand.{/idea} Do what is right, and rely on Him.
old: Powerful people's plans are unstoppable.
new: Every plot, however big, is known to Allah and within His control.
try: When you feel outmatched today, say: Hasbunallahu wa ni'mal wakeel.

title: Allah never breaks His promise to His messengers.
subtitle: A promise of victory that cannot fail
then: After the warnings, a firm assurance. Ibn Kathir says {reward}Allah promised His messengers victory in this life and on the Day the witnesses come forth{/reward}. {idea}Nothing He wills escapes Him, and none can resist Him.{/idea}
now: You are holding on to a promise of Allah: that hardship comes with ease, that He answers dua. It has been a long wait. {reward}His promises do not expire.{/reward}
old: Maybe Allah's promises are not meant for someone like me.
new: Allah never breaks a promise, and I can wait for it with trust.
try: Write down one promise of Allah you are holding onto, and read it once each day this week.

title: A Day when the earth becomes another earth.
subtitle: Everything familiar replaced, all creation before the One
then: Ibn Kathir cites Bukhari and Muslim: {idea}people will be gathered on a white, flat earth, like a round of bread, with no landmark for anyone{/idea}. Aishah asked the Prophet ﷺ where people will be then. {reward}He said: on the Sirat.{/reward}
now: Your street, your house, the café where you meet friends: you could walk them with your eyes closed. One day none of it will be there. {idea}Only the One will remain to face.{/idea}
old: The world I know is solid and permanent.
new: Even the earth will change; only Allah remains, and I will stand before Him.
try: On your walk today, look at one familiar place and remember it will not last, but your deeds will.

title: The guilty, bound together with their like.
subtitle: People gathered with those they resembled

row.title: we are gathered with our like

then: On that changed earth, Ibn Kathir says, {trap}the criminals will be bound together, each with his like{/trap}. He links it to: assemble those who did wrong together with their companions. It describes the Day soberly, as a warning.
now: Look at the five people you spend most time with, online and off. They shape what you laugh at, what you skip, what you think is normal. {idea}People are gathered with those they resemble.{/idea}
old: My friends do not affect who I become.
new: I am drawn toward those I keep close, so I choose them carefully.
try: Spend time today with one person who reminds you of Allah.

title: Clothed in what burns.
subtitle: The garment of those who refused
then: Ibn Kathir says the pitch mentioned is a substance {trap}quick to catch fire{/trap}, used in his time to coat camels. The verse is short and stark. It is a warning, said so that people in Makkah, and listeners after them, {idea}would turn back while they could{/idea}.
now: You spend real time choosing clothes: for work, for Eid, for a wedding. You think about how they will look. {idea}Think also about what your deeds are dressing you in.{/idea} That garment is chosen every day.
old: What I wear is about how I look to people.
new: My deeds are a garment too, and I can choose a good one now.
try: As you get dressed tomorrow, ask Allah to clothe you in taqwa.

title: Every soul repaid for exactly what it earned.
subtitle: Justice, and swift reckoning

row.title: too many to judge
sub: I will be lost in the crowd

row.title: swift reckoning
sub: all like one soul to Him

then: The scenes of that Day have a purpose: {idea}that Allah may repay each soul for what it earned{/idea}. Ibn Kathir says He is swift in reckoning because He knows everything; {idea}His power over all creation is the same as over one{/idea}.
now: You assume that among billions, your small lie or your quiet kindness will get lost. {reward}Nothing gets lost.{/reward} The coin you gave, the word you held back, all counted, quickly and fairly.
old: With so many people, my small deeds will not be noticed.
new: Every soul, including mine, is repaid exactly and swiftly.
try: Do one small good deed today knowing that it is counted.

title: This Quran is a message for all people.
subtitle: Warning, Oneness, and a reminder for the thoughtful
then: The surah closes where it began. Verse 1 said the Book brings mankind from darkness into light. Ibn Kathir says {idea}this Quran is a message for all mankind and jinn{/idea}, so they may be warned, {idea}know that He is One God{/idea}, and so the thoughtful will take heed.
now: You just finished reading Surah Ibrahim on a screen in your hand, centuries after it was first recited in Makkah. {reward}It reached you.{/reward} That means it was sent to you.
old: The Quran was addressed to people long ago.
new: The Quran is a message for whoever it reaches, and it has reached me.
try: Pick one verse from Surah Ibrahim that stayed with you, and share it with someone today.
